questions.question_text: A consumer's total utility from 1 to 5 units of a good is 12, 22, 30, 36, 40. The marginal utility of the fourth unit is:
For the same schedule, the average utility from four units is:
A consumer's marginal utilities from successive units are 20, 14, 8, 2, −3. Total utility is maximum after the:
questions.explanation: TU is highest where MU is still positive and next MU turns negative; the sum is highest after the 4th unit (44).

questions.question_text: When marginal utility is positive but falling, total utility:
questions.explanation: Each extra unit still adds to TU, but by less.

questions.question_text: Which statement about the point of satiety is correct?
options: MU equals price and TU is zero
MU is negative and TU is maximum
MU is maximum and TU is zero
MU is zero and TU is at its maximum
questions.explanation: Additional consumption adds nothing at satiety.

questions.question_text: The law of diminishing marginal utility assumes that:
options: Units consumed are of different sizes and qualities
Consumer income rises with each unit
Consumption is continuous and the consumer's taste is unchanged
The marginal utility of money keeps changing
questions.explanation: Standard identical units, continuous consumption and constant tastes are assumed.

questions.question_text: A collector's satisfaction from each additional rare stamp rises as the set nears completion. This is an:
options: Exception to the law of DMU
Application of the law of DMU
questions.explanation: Collections and hobbies can show increasing marginal utility.

questions.question_text: The diamond–water paradox is explained by distinguishing:
questions.explanation: Water has high total but low marginal utility due to abundance.

questions.question_text: Progressive taxation is justified using diminishing marginal utility on the ground that:
options: The poor save a larger share of their incomes than the rich
The rich consume a wider range of goods than the poor
A rupee gives the same utility to the rich and the poor
The marginal utility of money falls as income rises
questions.explanation: A rupee of tax costs a rich person less satisfaction than a poor person.

questions.question_text: A consumer buys X at Rs 4 (MU = 24) and Y at Rs 6 (MU = 30). He should:
options: Buy more of Y and less of X
Buy more of X and less of Y
questions.explanation: MUx/Px = 6 > MUy/Py = 5, so X gives more utility per rupee.

questions.question_text: A consumer is in equilibrium with MUx = 18 and Px = Rs 3. The marginal utility of a rupee (MUm) is:
questions.explanation: MUx/Px = MUm = 18/3.

questions.question_text: If MUx/Px = 8 and MUy/Py = 8 and the consumer spends all income, then:
options: He should buy more of Y
He is spending more than income
He should buy more of X
questions.explanation: Equal marginal utility per rupee means no reallocation gains.

questions.question_text: A consumer is willing to pay Rs 50 for the first unit, Rs 40 for the second and Rs 30 for the third. Price is Rs 30 and he buys 3 units. Consumer surplus is:
If a consumer pays Rs 35 for a book he values at Rs 50, his consumer surplus is:
questions.explanation: Willingness to pay minus price paid.

questions.question_text: Which factor most clearly weakens the measurement of consumer surplus?
options: The income of the consumer is always positive
The market price of the good is fixed for all buyers
The marginal utility of money does not stay constant
The quantity bought is measured in discrete units
questions.explanation: Marshall assumed a constant MU of money; in reality it changes with income and spending.

questions.question_text: The cardinal approach to utility is associated with:
questions.explanation: Marshall used measurable utility in utils.

questions.question_text: The ordinal approach needs the consumer to:
options: Rank bundles in order of preference
Spend all income on one good
Know the marginal utility of money
questions.explanation: It requires only ranking.

questions.question_text: An indifference curve shows combinations of two goods that yield:
questions.explanation: The consumer is indifferent among them.

questions.question_text: Along an indifference curve, MRS of X for Y falls because:
options: With more X held, the consumer will give up less Y per extra X
The budget line gets flatter as quantity of X increases
The price of X is falling as more is bought
The consumer's income rises as he moves down the curve
questions.explanation: X becomes less valuable relative to Y as its quantity rises.

questions.question_text: MRSxy equals:
questions.explanation: MRSxy = MUx/MUy.

questions.question_text: Two indifference curves cannot intersect because the intersection would:
options: Give two satisfaction levels to one bundle, violating transitivity
Make the two curves parallel at every other point
Turn the slope of both curves from negative to positive
Imply a change in the consumer's money income
questions.explanation: Consistent preferences forbid it.

questions.question_text: If two goods are perfect substitutes, the indifference curve is:
options: A straight line with constant MRS
Convex to the origin with falling MRS
Concave to the origin with rising MRS
questions.explanation: The consumer substitutes at a constant rate.

questions.question_text: Right shoes and left shoes are best represented by indifference curves that are:
questions.explanation: Perfect complements are used in fixed proportions.

questions.question_text: Income is Rs 600, Px = Rs 20 and Py = Rs 30. The maximum quantity of Y that can be bought is:
With M = 600, Px = 20, Py = 30, the slope of the budget line is:
questions.explanation: Slope = −Px/Py = −20/30.

questions.question_text: A rise in income with constant prices shifts the budget line:
questions.explanation: Both intercepts rise proportionately.

questions.question_text: A fall in Px with M and Py constant makes the budget line:
questions.explanation: The X-intercept M/Px rises.

questions.question_text: If both prices double and income doubles, the budget line:
questions.explanation: Real income is unchanged.

questions.question_text: A point lying inside the budget line means that the bundle is:
options: Costing exactly the whole of income
Affordable with some income left unspent
The best bundle on the highest indifference curve
questions.explanation: Its cost is below income.

questions.question_text: Consumer equilibrium in the ordinal approach occurs where:
options: IC and budget lines are parallel at all points
The budget line is tangent to the highest attainable IC
The budget line cuts an indifference curve
questions.explanation: MRS equals the price ratio at the tangency.

questions.question_text: At equilibrium MRSxy = 2 and Px = Rs 10. Therefore Py is:
questions.explanation: MRS = Px/Py → 2 = 10/Py.

questions.question_text: If MRSxy > Px/Py, the consumer should:
options: Buy more Y and less X
Buy more X and less Y
questions.explanation: He values X more than the market does.

questions.question_text: The second-order (sufficient) condition for consumer equilibrium in the ordinal approach is that:
options: Utility is at its maximum for each good separately
The budget line is a straight line with a negative slope
The IC is convex to the origin where it touches the budget line
MRS equals the ratio of prices at the chosen bundle
questions.explanation: MRS must be diminishing at the tangency.

questions.question_text: A corner solution occurs when the consumer:
options: Buys both goods in equal quantity
Spends all income on one good only
questions.explanation: The tangency condition fails at an axis.

questions.question_text: The income-consumption curve joins equilibrium points as:
options: Both prices change in the same proportion
The price of X changes with income and Y constant
Tastes change with prices and income constant
Income changes while prices stay constant
questions.explanation: ICC traces the effect of income on the consumer's choice.

questions.question_text: For an inferior good, the income-consumption curve:
questions.explanation: Consumption falls as income rises beyond a point.

questions.question_text: The Engel curve relates:
questions.explanation: Derived from the ICC.

questions.question_text: The price-consumption curve is used to derive the:
questions.explanation: Plot price against quantity at each equilibrium.

questions.question_text: The price effect is equal to:
questions.explanation: Price effect has two parts.

questions.question_text: When the price of a good falls, the substitution effect on the quantity demanded of that good is:
options: Negative in the price–quantity sense: more of it is bought
Positive in direction, as the consumer buys less of it
Ambiguous, depending on whether the good is inferior
Zero, because real income is held constant
questions.explanation: It always moves quantity opposite to price.

questions.question_text: For a normal good, the income effect of a fall in its price works:
options: More strongly than the price effect taken together
With zero effect, as real income is unchanged
Against the substitution effect, reducing the quantity
In the same direction as the substitution effect
questions.explanation: Both increase the quantity demanded.

questions.question_text: A Giffen good is one for which:
options: Demand is perfectly elastic at the going price
Both the substitution and income effects are positive
A strong negative income effect outweighs the substitution effect
The substitution effect outweighs a weak income effect
questions.explanation: Quantity demanded rises when price rises.

questions.question_text: Which statement is true of a Giffen good?
options: It is an inferior good taking a large share of income
It is a luxury good bought for prestige and status
It is a normal good with high income elasticity
It has a negative price effect like other goods
questions.explanation: Giffen goods are strongly inferior and important in the budget.

questions.question_text: According to the ordinal analysis, the demand curve slopes downward for:
options: No class of goods, since utility cannot be measured
Normal goods and inferior goods with a weak income effect
Giffen goods only and for no other class
questions.explanation: The substitution effect dominates.

questions.question_text: The cardinal condition for equilibrium with two goods is MUx/Px = MUy/Py = MUm. The ordinal condition MRS = Px/Py is equivalent because:
questions.explanation: Combining gives MUx/MUy = Px/Py.

questions.question_text: A consumer buys 10 units of a good at price Rs 5 and MU of the 10th unit is 20 utils. MU of money is:
After the price of a good falls, the consumer is again in equilibrium when:
options: MU of the good is greater than the new price
MU of the good equals the new price, in terms of MU of money
TU of the good equals the new price
MU of the good is less than the new price
questions.explanation: He buys more until MU falls to the lower price.

questions.question_text: The law of equi-marginal utility finds application in:
options: The lending decisions of commercial banks alone
Consumption, production and public finance decisions
The taxation decisions of the government alone
questions.explanation: It applies wherever limited resources are allocated among uses.

questions.question_text: A student allocates study hours among subjects so that the extra marks per hour are equal. This follows:
questions.explanation: Allocation to equalise marginal returns.

questions.question_text: Which is an assumption of the law of equi-marginal utility?
options: The consumer chooses without any rational plan
Income is limited and MU of money stays constant
The goods consumed are perfect complements
Utility is only ranked and cannot be measured
questions.explanation: Limited income and constant MU of money.

questions.question_text: A consumer's income is Rs 100. Px = Rs 10, Py = Rs 20. He buys 4 units of X and 3 units of Y. His budget is:
questions.explanation: 4×10 + 3×20 = 100; on the budget line.

questions.question_text: Price of X rises from Rs 10 to Rs 20 while M = 200 and Py = 10. The new maximum X is:
The slope of an IC at a point equals:
questions.explanation: The slope's absolute value is the MRS.

questions.question_text: In the diagram, an IC higher than another IC represents:
questions.explanation: More of at least one good.

questions.question_text: Indifference curves do not touch the axes because:
options: The consumer buys both goods in positive amounts
The MRS stays constant along the curve
The two goods are available free of charge
The consumer's income is equal to zero
questions.explanation: Touching an axis would mean that one good is not consumed at all.

questions.question_text: Which statement about indifference curves is FALSE?
options: They are parallel to each other
They are convex to the origin
questions.explanation: ICs need not be parallel.

questions.question_text: Suppose a consumer's equilibrium bundle is on IC2. If income rises and he moves to IC3, the new equilibrium lies:
questions.explanation: A parallel outward shift of the budget line.

questions.question_text: The demand curve derived from the PCC slopes downward for a normal good because:
options: Utility is measured cardinally in utils
The price effect on quantity is exactly zero
The substitution and income effects work in the same direction
Only the income effect operates on quantity
questions.explanation: Both raise quantity demanded when price falls.

questions.question_text: The main advantage of the ordinal approach over the cardinal approach is that it:
options: Needs no measurable utility or constant MU of money
Requires budget lines and not indifference curves
Uses total utility curves for each good
questions.explanation: It uses ranking only.

questions.question_text: If the marginal utility of good X is 12 and Y is 18, and Px = Rs 2, Py = Rs 3, the consumer:
A rise in income from Rs 1,000 to Rs 1,500 lowers the quantity of bajra consumed from 20 kg to 15 kg. Bajra is:
questions.explanation: Quantity falls as income rises.

questions.question_text: The income elasticity of an inferior good is:
questions.explanation: Demand falls as income rises.

questions.question_text: Which is a limitation of consumer surplus?
options: MU of money is not constant
questions.explanation: The concept assumes constant MU of money.

questions.question_text: Consumer surplus for a good with a straight-line demand curve D: P = 100 − Q and price 40 is:
questions.explanation: Triangle with base 60 and height 60 = ½ × 60 × 60.

questions.question_text: If price rises, consumer surplus generally:
questions.explanation: The area between demand and price shrinks.

questions.question_text: The substitution effect holds constant:
questions.explanation: It isolates the effect of relative price change.

questions.question_text: When the price of X falls, the budget line pivots outward on the X-axis. The new tangent IC is:
questions.explanation: Real income has risen.

questions.question_text: Which pair is correct?
options: Ordinal approach – MU of money constant
questions.explanation: The cardinal approach assumes measurable utility.

questions.question_text: A consumer maximises satisfaction when the last rupee spent on each good gives:
options: Maximum total utility for each good
questions.explanation: Equal MU per rupee.

questions.question_text: A consumer finds 3 units of Y exactly as satisfying as 1 unit of X at every point. His IC for X and Y is:
options: Vertical at one quantity of X
A straight line with a slope of −3
questions.explanation: Constant MRS = 3.

questions.question_text: The budget constraint implies that:
options: Total spending on both goods cannot exceed income
Expenditure may exceed income if prices fall
Prices of goods are set by the consumer's income
Income depends on the prices of the two goods
questions.explanation: M ≥ Px·X + Py·Y.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is NOT affected by a change in income, ceteris paribus?
questions.explanation: Slope depends on the price ratio.

questions.question_text: A consumer's MRS of X for Y is 4 and price ratio Px/Py = 2. To reach equilibrium he should:
questions.explanation: MRS > price ratio: the consumer values X more than the market asks.

questions.question_text: The first-order condition for consumer equilibrium is that:
options: The slope of the IC equals the slope of the budget line
MUx equals MUy for the two goods
The budget line is a vertical straight line
The IC is convex to the origin at that point
questions.explanation: MRS equals the price ratio.

questions.question_text: Why does the first unit of a good give more utility than the second?
options: Returns to scale are increasing for later units
Most urgent want is met first, later wants are weaker
Its price is higher than that of later units
The consumer's income is lower for later units
questions.explanation: Successive wants are less intense.

questions.question_text: If TU is 30 for 3 units and 38 for 4 units, then MU of the 4th unit is:
A consumer is indifferent between bundles A (6X, 2Y) and B (4X, 4Y). MRS between A and B is:
questions.explanation: ΔY = 2 for ΔX = 2 gives MRS = 1.

questions.question_text: A consumer spends Rs 100 on X (Px = 20) and Y (Py = 10) buying 2X and 6Y. His budget is:
Normal goods have an ICC that:
questions.explanation: More income means more quantity.

questions.question_text: Which statement correctly states Gossen's second law?
options: Income is allocated so that MU per rupee is equal across goods
MU equals the price for each good considered separately
MU from a good diminishes as more units are consumed
Total utility is maximum when MU is zero for a good
questions.explanation: Equi-marginal utility.

questions.question_text: A consumer treats left and right gloves as perfect complements. If the price of left gloves rises, he will:
options: Leave his purchases of both gloves unchanged
Cut down purchases of both gloves in proportion
Buy only right gloves from now on
Buy more left gloves to make up for the loss
questions.explanation: Complements are used in fixed proportions.

questions.question_text: If a good has a negative price effect only through its substitution effect and zero income effect, then:
questions.explanation: Only the substitution effect operates.

questions.question_text: A rise in the price of tea, with coffee as a substitute, will move the consumer's demand for coffee:
questions.explanation: Substitution towards coffee.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is true under the ordinal approach?
options: Utility can be added across goods
questions.explanation: Consistent ranking is assumed.

questions.question_text: Which statement is TRUE of the budget line?
options: Its slope is the ratio of prices
questions.explanation: Slope = −Px/Py.

questions.question_text: Using the ordinal analysis, the demand curve for X shows:
options: Price–quantity combinations at which the consumer is in equilibrium
Bundles of X and Y that give equal satisfaction to the consumer
Combinations of production cost and quantity of X supplied
Combinations of income and quantity of X purchased
questions.explanation: It is derived from points on the price-consumption curve.

questions.question_text: The consumer has Rs 240 and buys X at Rs 8 and Y at Rs 6. If he buys 15 units of X, the maximum units of Y he can buy is:
In consumer equilibrium, MUx/MUy equals:
questions.explanation: The ratio of marginal utilities equals the price ratio.

questions.question_text: A consumer buys 5 units of apples and 4 of oranges. MU of the last apple is 15 and orange 20 with prices Rs 3 and Rs 5. He is:
options: Under-consuming apples and should buy more
Over-consuming apples and should buy fewer apples
questions.explanation: 15/3 = 5 > 20/5 = 4, so more apples.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following is an application of the law of DMU?
questions.explanation: Lower MU means willingness to pay falls with quantity.

questions.question_text: As income increases, the consumer moves from an IC to a higher IC, and the budget line shifts:
questions.explanation: Parallel outward.

questions.question_text: Which is a reason for the downward slope of an indifference curve?
options: More of one good must be offset by less of the other to hold satisfaction
The consumer's income is rising as he moves along it
The prices of the two goods are constant everywhere
MRS is diminishing along the curve
questions.explanation: Otherwise satisfaction would change.

questions.question_text: A consumer's bundle lies on a lower indifference curve than one he can reach on his budget line. He:
options: Is spending more than his income
Can gain by moving to a bundle on a higher IC
Has no income to spend on goods
questions.explanation: He is not maximising satisfaction.

questions.question_text: A good is a luxury if its income elasticity is:
questions.explanation: Quantity rises more than proportionately with income.

questions.question_text: The ordinal approach is considered more realistic because:
options: Consumers can rank preferences without assigning numbers
Prices of the goods are fixed by the producers
Income is fixed over the period of choice
Consumers can measure utility exactly in utils
questions.explanation: Ranking is easier than measuring.

questions.question_text: The marginal utility per rupee of X is 8 and of Y is 6. If the price of X falls, MUx/Px will:
questions.explanation: A lower price raises MU per rupee.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a reason why the demand curve for Giffen goods slopes upward?
questions.explanation: Real income falls on price rise, so more of the good is bought.

questions.question_text: Which of these combinations lies exactly on the budget line M = 100, Px = 10, Py = 5?
questions.explanation: 5×10 + 10×5 = 100; the others cost 105, 90 and 90.

questions.question_text: On the budget line, an extra unit of X can be had only by giving up Px/Py units of Y. This ratio is:
options: The total utility from X and Y
The opportunity cost of X in terms of Y
questions.explanation: Price ratio is the market opportunity cost.

questions.question_text: The law of DMU helps derive the demand curve because:
options: Price is constant at every quantity
At equilibrium MU equals price, so the MU curve traces demand
TU always equals the price in the market
Income is constant at every price
questions.explanation: The downward-sloping MU curve becomes the demand curve.
